lesson.title: W-Word Cognate Set
lesson.subtitle: All eight W-words matched to their English twins — and the wer≠where trap

hook.title: Eight Words, One Ancient Family
hook.content: Here is the full set, laid out on one table: was (what), wo (where), wer (who), wann (when), wie (how/why), warum (wherefore), wohin (whither), and — for the return trip — woher (whence, 'where-from'). English whittled this family down to a handful of survivors; German kept every branch. Both languages spelled the ancient hw- their own way: English wh-, German w-. Which means every German W-word is your own question word, one letter and one dropped h away.

footnotes.title: The Missing Eighth Twin
footnotes.content: woher (from where?) is the twin of whence — 'where-from'. WOHER kommst du? asks where you are coming FROM, and WOHIN gehst du? asks where you are going TO. whence/whither, woher/wohin — both languages once kept the full four-way compass.

pattern.title: The Trap Is Built In
pattern.content: The trap: WER looks like WHERE but asks WHO. WO looks like WHO (or 'woe') but asks WHERE. The twins are honest — wer ↔ who (one dropped h, an a→e vowel drift), wo ↔ where — but the shapes swapped. Then the drift words: wie covers 'how' (though its root is why's — English split one word into how and why), warum is the wherefore twin, wann is when with the hw- intact as w-. Drill the set until the trap disarms itself: wer=who, wo=where, never crossed.
pattern.linguist_note: All eight descend from the Proto-Indo-European interrogative *kʷi/*kʷo — the same stem that gave Latin qu- words (quid, quo, quando). English who/what/when/where/why/whether/which and German wer/was/wann/wo/welch are one family tree, split across two alphabets.

exercises.prompt: The full set — match each W-word with its twin. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: was, wann, warum, wohin, wo ist der Hund, wer kennt das Tier, wie kurz, wer kommt nie, Wir sind leise, Wir wollen das wissen, Wir kennen das Tier, meine Tasse
exercises.meaning: what; when; why / wherefore; whither (where to); where is the dog; who knows the animal; how short; who never comes; We are quiet; We want to know that; We know the animal; my cup
exercises.explanation: One ancient family: English wh-, German w-, one dropped h between them — and the W-words take any verb or noun you own along: kennen (to know a thing or person) included.

exercises.prompt: Trap drill: 'Wer kommt?' — what is being asked?
exercises.explanation: wer ↔ who: the a→e drift moved the vowel, never the meaning. wo is where; wer is who. And the answer can be nothing at all: Was weißt du? — Nichts.

exercises.prompt: Trap drill, remixed: 'Warum ist das Getränk nicht billig?' — what is being asked?
options: WHERE is the drink not cheap?
WHY is the drink not cheap?
WHO is the drink not cheap?
WHEN is the drink not cheap?
exercises.target_answer: WHY is the drink not cheap?
exercises.explanation: warum ↔ wherefore — 'for what'. The lookalike trap works in both directions: wo looks like who, warum sounds like warm — the meaning lives in the -um.

exercises.reply_idea: Reply that the book is here.
cues: Put ist in second position, then hier.
exercises.explanation: Wo asks where; your reply keeps the verb ist in second position: Das Buch ist hier.
W-question, verb second, then the subject — and whatever adjectives you own (laut, leise, kurz, billig) can ride in the wie-slot.

summary.outcome: Recall all eight W-words with their twins and defeat the wer/wo trap.
summary.takeaway: The W-words are one family — English wh-, German w- — and the trap is structural: wer=who, wo=where.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: No-do-support Drills — transform statements into questions with the verb flip alone.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from W-Word Cognate Set (How loud is the cat):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wie laut ist die Katze" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of W-Word Cognate Set without relying on short-term echo.

wo.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwēr/*hwar — the exact twin of English where; English kept the h (wh-), German dropped it. [wiktionary]

wer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwaz — the exact twin of English who. The famous trap: wer asks WHO, wo asks WHERE. [wiktionary]

wann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwan — the exact twin of English when. [wiktionary]

wie.context_translation: How are you? (How goes it to you?)
wie.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hwē, a fossilized instrumental of who/what — the same variant that gave English why. [wiktionary]

warum.etymology_derivation: wo + um — 'around-what / for-what', the structural twin of English wherefore ('for what'). [wiktionary]

wohin.context_translation: Where are you going (whither goest thou)?
wohin.etymology_derivation: wo + hin; hin is the twin of the h- in English hence/hither — 'to where' in one word. [wiktionary]

katze.context_phrase: Die Katze schläft auf dem Sofa.
katze.context_translation: The cat sleeps on the sofa.

hund.context_phrase: Der Hund schläft auf dem Sofa.
hund.context_translation: The dog sleeps on the sofa.
hund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaz — cognate with English hound, the same ancient dog-word. [wiktionary]

kennen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *kannijaną, a causative of *kunnaną (can); the page lists English ken (as in beyond my ken) — the same knowing-verb English keeps in Scotland. [wiktionary]

tier.etymology_derivation: From Old High German tior, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from PIE *dʰewsóm. English deer is the listed cognate; the Germanic d appears as t in High German. [wiktionary]

kurz.etymology_derivation: From Latin curtus — the same Latin word as English curt; NOT related to short. [wiktionary]

laut.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hlūd; only Old Saxon hlūd compared — the loud link is not on the page. [wiktionary]

leise.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *līs(ī) 'low, soft'; no cognates named — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

billig.etymology_derivation: Old High German billīh 'appropriate', kin to Bild/bilden; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

nie.context_phrase: Ich habe nie Zeit am Montag.
nie.context_translation: I never have time on Monday.
nie.etymology_derivation: MHG nie, OHG nio; thin etymology on Wiktionary. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

nichts.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German nihtes niht, literally nothing of nothing — an emphatic doubling of niht 'not', just like French rien de rien. [wiktionary]

niemand.etymology_derivation: nie 'never' + Mann 'man': literally never-man — the page analyzes it exactly so, the same idea as English no man and none. [wiktionary]
